title: The Lighthouse · 13
paragraphs: “He must have reached it,” Lily Briscoe said aloud, and suddenly she felt utterly exhausted. For the Lighthouse had almost disappeared; it had dissolved into a blue haze. And the strain of looking at it, together with the strain of thinking of him landing there—which seemed to be one and the same strain—had pulled her body and her mind as far as they would go. Ah, but what relief she felt. Whatever it was she had wanted to give him when he left her that morning, she had given it to him at last.

“He has landed,” she said aloud. “It is finished.” Then old Mr. Carmichael heaved himself up, puffing a little, and stood beside her like some old pagan god, shaggy, weeds in his hair and the trident (it was only a French novel) in his hand. He stood next to her at the edge of the lawn, his great bulk swaying slightly, and, shading his eyes with his hand, said, “They will have landed,” and she felt she had been right. They had had no need to speak. They had been thinking the same things, and he had answered her without her asking him anything. There he stood, spreading his hands over all the frailty and suffering of mankind; she thought he was looking out, tolerantly, compassionately, over their final fate. Now he has crowned the occasion, she thought, as his hand slowly dropped—as though she had watched him let fall from his great height a wreath of violets and asphodels, which drifted slowly down and came to rest at last on the earth.

Quickly, as though something over there had called her back, she turned to her canvas. There it was—her picture. Yes, with all its greens and blues, its lines running upward and across, its attempt at something. It would be hung up in the attic, she thought; it would be destroyed. But what did that matter? she asked herself, and took up her brush once more. She looked at the steps: they were empty. She looked at her canvas: it was blurred. With a sudden intensity, as though for one second she saw it clearly, she drew a line there, in the center. It was done; it was finished. Yes, she thought, laying down her brush in extreme fatigue, I have had my vision.
